GraphQL can do everything REST can do → Partially false. While GraphQL has mutations for CRUD operations, REST may have specialized endpoints that don't have direct GraphQL equivalents (e.g., dedicated copy endpoints). For duplicating pages, REST's copy endpoint is more straightforward than GraphQL's query-then-create approach

Quick reference guide to the 3.5 mm (1/8 in) mini phone connector family, sometimes called the "mini-jack" or "mini audio jack"
A miniaturized version of the original 1/4 in (6.35 mm) phone connector
Same physical plug size across variants; the number of conductor bands (tip/ring/sleeve) determines what the connector can carry
Related Sizes (not covered in detail here)
2.5 mm (sub-mini): same tip/ring/sleeve concept, used on some older cordless phones and two-way radios
Related Sizes (not covered in detail here)
6.35 mm / 1/4 in (standard phone connector): the original size, common in professional audio (guitar cables, studio patch bays)
Related Sizes (not covered in detail here)
TRRS adds a mic/ground ring, but two incompatible wiring orders exist:
CTIA/AHJ (Apple, most modern Android/Windows devices): tip = left, ring 1 = right, ring 2 = ground, sleeve = mic
TRRS adds a mic/ground ring, but two incompatible wiring orders exist:
OMTP (older Nokia and some Asian-market phones): tip = left, ring 1 = right, ring 2 = mic, sleeve = ground
TRRS adds a mic/ground ring, but two incompatible wiring orders exist:
Plugging a headset wired to one standard into a jack wired to the other leaves left/right audio unaffected but the microphone silent, since only the mic/ground pair is swapped
Four contacts, three insulating rings. Adds a microphone and inline-remote contact to the stereo pair of Audio/Connector/Phone/TRS.
Two wiring orders are in circulation, CTIA/AHJ and OMTP. Both put left on the tip and right on the first ring, and they swap the microphone and ground between the second ring and the sleeve.
Five-contact successors exist: TRRRS at 3.5 mm under ITU-T P.382, adding a second microphone or a power line, and the 4.4 mm Pentaconn under JEITA RC-8141C for balanced headphone cable.
Audio/Connector/Phone/TRRS/3.5mm — phone and tablet headsets. Defined by JEITA/EIAJ RC-5325A.
Image: public domain (CC0), via Wikimedia Commons
TRRS stands for Tip-Ring-Ring-Sleeve: 4 conductors, 3 insulating rings
Extends Audio/Connector/Phone/TRS/3.5mm with a second ring, used to carry a microphone signal and/or inline remote-control signal (play/pause, volume, call answer)
Standard connector for phone/tablet headsets that combine stereo output with a microphone
CTIA/AHJ is used by Apple, most modern Android devices, and Windows laptops
OMTP was used by older Nokia phones and some Asian-market handsets

Plugging a headset wired to one standard into a jack wired to the other still passes left/right audio correctly (tip and ring 1 match), but the microphone does not work, since only the ring 2/sleeve pair is swapped
Fits into the same jack as Audio/Connector/Phone/TRS/3.5mm and Audio/Connector/Phone/TS/3.5mm plugs, which simply leave the extra ring(s) unconnected
Smartphone and tablet headsets (earbuds with in-line mic and remote)
Some cameras and action cams (external mic input, though wiring convention varies by manufacturer)
Three contacts, two insulating rings. The same plug serves two wirings, and the size and the gear decide which:
Unbalanced stereo — tip left, ring right, sleeve ground. The usual reading at 3.5 mm.
Three contacts, two insulating rings. The same plug serves two wirings, and the size and the gear decide which:
Balanced mono — tip and ring carry the two differential halves of one signal, sleeve the shield. The usual reading at 6.35 mm in professional audio.
Three contacts, two insulating rings. The same plug serves two wirings, and the size and the gear decide which:
A third wiring appears on mixing desks, where one TRS jack is an unbalanced insert point carrying send on the tip and return on the ring.
Audio/Connector/Phone/TRS/3.5mm — headphones, earbuds, and aux and line cabling.
6.35 mm (1/4 in) — balanced line and insert cabling, and a compact substitute for XLR on small mixing desks.
Image: public domain (CC0), via Wikimedia Commons
TRS stands for Tip-Ring-Sleeve: 3 conductors, 2 insulating rings
At 3.5 mm, TRS almost always carries unbalanced stereo audio — this is the standard headphone/aux plug
At 1/4 in, the same tip/ring/sleeve layout is more often used for balanced mono audio in professional gear; the connotation differs by size and context
